title: Energetics
description: Exothermic and endothermic reactions, interpreting and drawing reaction pathway diagrams, activation energy, and bond-energy calculations of ΔH for IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (Core and Extended tiers).

notes.heading: Exothermic Reactions
notes.body:
📌 Definition
An **exothermic** reaction transfers energy to the surroundings — the surroundings get HOTTER and a thermometer in the mixture shows a temperature RISE.

🔑 Examples to quote
• **Combustion** of fuels: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O releases a large amount of energy.
• **Neutralisation**: acid + alkali → salt + water, and the mixture warms up.
• **Respiration** in living cells releases energy from glucose.

🔑 Everyday uses
Self-heating cans of coffee and disposable hand warmers both use exothermic reactions to warm their contents.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying 'the reaction gets hotter'. It is the SURROUNDINGS that gain energy — describe it as 'energy is transferred to the surroundings, so the temperature rises'.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Exothermic = energy out = temperature of surroundings goes UP.
• Combustion and neutralisation are the two classic exam examples.

notes.heading: Endothermic Reactions
notes.body:
📌 Definition
An **endothermic** reaction takes in energy from the surroundings — the surroundings get COLDER and a thermometer shows a temperature FALL.

🔑 Examples to quote
• **Thermal decomposition**: heating calcium carbonate, CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, needs a constant input of heat or the reaction stops.
• **Dissolving ammonium nitrate** in water — the mixture cools noticeably.
• **Photosynthesis** takes in light energy.

🔑 Everyday use
Sports-injury cold packs mix ammonium nitrate with water; the endothermic dissolving pulls energy out of the surroundings — including the injured muscle.

💡 The test
If the container feels cold, energy is being taken IN (endothermic). If it feels hot, energy is being given OUT (exothermic).

⚠️ Common Mistake
Confusing the two suffixes: exo = exit (energy leaves), endo = in (energy enters).

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Endothermic = energy in = temperature of surroundings goes DOWN.
• Thermal decomposition and NH₄NO₃ dissolving are the classic exam examples.

notes.heading: Reading Reaction Pathway Diagrams
notes.body:
A **reaction pathway diagram** (energy level diagram) plots the energy of the chemicals as the reaction proceeds. For Core, you must INTERPRET a given diagram.

🔑 How to read it
• The vertical axis is **energy**; the horizontal axis is the **progress of the reaction**.
• Find the reactants' level and the products' level.
• **Products LOWER than reactants** → energy has been given out → the reaction is **exothermic**.
• **Products HIGHER than reactants** → energy has been taken in → the reaction is **endothermic**.
• The vertical gap between the two levels is the overall energy change.

💡 Worked Example
A diagram shows reactants high on the energy axis and products lower, with a hump between them. The drop from reactants to products means energy is released — exothermic — consistent with a combustion reaction.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Reading the diagram backwards: the hump in the middle is NOT the energy change. Compare only the START (reactants) and END (products) levels for the overall change.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Products below reactants = exothermic; products above = endothermic.
• The diagram's vertical gap shows the size of the energy change.

illustration.alt: Two reaction pathway diagrams: an exothermic reaction with products lower in energy than reactants, and an endothermic reaction with products higher in energy than reactants, both showing the activation energy hump.
illustration.caption: Exothermic: products sit lower, so ΔH is negative. Endothermic: products sit higher, so ΔH is positive. The hump is the activation energy.

notes.heading: ΔH and Activation Energy (Extended tier)
notes.body:
📌 Definitions (Extended tier)
• **ΔH** (the enthalpy change) is the overall energy change of a reaction: energy of products minus energy of reactants, measured in **kJ/mol**.
• Exothermic reactions have a **NEGATIVE** ΔH (energy is lost to the surroundings); endothermic reactions have a **POSITIVE** ΔH.
• The **activation energy, Eₐ**, is the minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to occur.

🔑 Why exothermic reactions still need a push
Even a strongly exothermic reaction like burning methane needs a spark: the reactant bonds must be broken before new bonds can form, and that needs the activation energy first. Eₐ is always positive.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing ΔH without a sign, or with the wrong sign. 'Releases 698 kJ/mol' must be written as $\Delta H = -698\text{ kJ/mol}$ — the negative sign carries the direction of energy transfer.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• ΔH negative = exothermic; ΔH positive = endothermic. Unit: kJ/mol.
• Eₐ is the energy hump the reactants must get over — always positive.

notes.heading: Drawing Pathway Diagrams (Extended tier)
notes.body:
Extended-tier questions ask you to DRAW and label the diagram, not just read one. This is the sequence that picks up every mark.

🔑 The five steps
1. Draw and label the axes: **energy** (y) and **progress of reaction** (x).
2. Draw a horizontal line for the **reactants**.
3. Draw a second horizontal line for the **products** — BELOW the reactants for exothermic, ABOVE for endothermic.
4. Draw a curve that rises from reactants to a peak (the hump) and falls to the products.
5. Add arrows: **Eₐ** from the reactants' level UP to the peak, and **ΔH** from the reactants' level to the products' level.

💡 Exam detail
Label each arrow with its name AND, for ΔH, its sign — e.g. 'ΔH = −698 kJ/mol' on the downward arrow for an exothermic reaction.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Drawing the ΔH arrow from the PEAK to the products. ΔH compares reactants with products only; the peak belongs to the Eₐ arrow.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Eₐ: reactants → peak. ΔH: reactants → products.
• Products lower = exothermic (ΔH negative); products higher = endothermic (ΔH positive).

notes.heading: Bond Breaking and Bond Making (Extended tier)
notes.body:
📌 The two halves of every reaction
• **Breaking bonds ABSORBS energy** — it is an endothermic process. Energy must be supplied to pull atoms apart.
• **Making bonds RELEASES energy** — it is an exothermic process. Atoms give out energy as they join.

🔑 How a reaction gets its ΔH
Every reaction breaks the reactants' bonds and makes the products' bonds:
• If making releases MORE than breaking absorbs → net release → **exothermic** (ΔH negative).
• If breaking absorbs MORE than making releases → net absorption → **endothermic** (ΔH positive).

💡 Worked Example
A reaction absorbs $2840\text{ kJ/mol}$ breaking bonds and releases $2450\text{ kJ/mol}$ making bonds. More energy went in than came out, so the reaction is endothermic with $\Delta H = 2840 - 2450 = +390\text{ kJ/mol}$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying 'bond breaking releases energy'. It is the single most common energetics error: BREAKING takes energy IN, MAKING lets energy OUT.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Break = absorb (endothermic); make = release (exothermic).
• The overall ΔH is the balance of the two.

notes.heading: Calculating ΔH from Bond Energies (Extended tier)
notes.body:
📌 The formula
$$\Delta H = \Sigma E_{\text{broken}} - \Sigma E_{\text{made}}$$
Bond energies (in kJ/mol) are given in the question. Count every bond, multiplied by how many molecules are involved.

💡 Worked Example 1 — combustion of methane
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, using C–H $412$, O=O $496$, C=O $743$, O–H $463\text{ kJ/mol}$.
• Bonds broken: $4 \times 412 + 2 \times 496 = 1648 + 992 = 2640\text{ kJ/mol}$
• Bonds made: $2 \times 743 + 4 \times 463 = 1486 + 1852 = 3338\text{ kJ/mol}$
$$\begin{aligned} \Delta H &= 2640 - 3338 \\ &= -698\text{ kJ/mol} \end{aligned}$$
Negative — combustion is exothermic, as expected.

💡 Worked Example 2 — hydrogen + chlorine
H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl, using H–H $436$, Cl–Cl $242$, H–Cl $431\text{ kJ/mol}$.
• Broken: $436 + 242 = 678\text{ kJ/mol}$; made: $2 \times 431 = 862\text{ kJ/mol}$
• $\Delta H = 678 - 862 = -184\text{ kJ/mol}$ (exothermic).

⚠️ Common Mistake
Swapping the subtraction (made − broken gives the wrong sign), or forgetting that '2HCl' means TWO H–Cl bonds. Write out the bond count for every molecule before you add.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• ΔH = broken − made, in kJ/mol.
• A negative answer is exothermic — check the sign against the chemistry as a sanity test.

flashcards.definition: A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises.
flashcards.example: Combustion of methane; neutralisation of an acid by an alkali.

flashcards.definition: A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
flashcards.example: Thermal decomposition of CaCO₃; dissolving ammonium nitrate in water.

flashcards.definition: The products are drawn LOWER in energy than the reactants; the drop is the energy released.
flashcards.example: A combustion diagram shows reactants high and products low.

flashcards.definition: The products are drawn HIGHER in energy than the reactants; the rise is the energy absorbed.
flashcards.example: A thermal decomposition diagram shows products above reactants.

flashcards.definition: The overall energy change of a reaction (products minus reactants), in kJ/mol. Negative for exothermic, positive for endothermic (Extended).
The minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to occur (Extended).
flashcards.example: A spark supplies the Eₐ needed to start methane burning.

flashcards.definition: An ENDOTHERMIC process — energy must be absorbed to pull bonded atoms apart (Extended).
flashcards.example: Breaking the four C–H bonds in CH₄ absorbs 4 × 412 = 1648 kJ/mol.

flashcards.definition: An EXOTHERMIC process — energy is released when new bonds form (Extended).
flashcards.example: Forming two H–Cl bonds releases 2 × 431 = 862 kJ/mol.

flashcards.definition: ΔH = (energy to break bonds) − (energy released making bonds), in kJ/mol (Extended).
Hand warmers and self-heating cans use exothermic reactions; sports cold packs use an endothermic process such as NH₄NO₃ dissolving.
flashcards.example: The cold pack feels cold because dissolving takes energy from your skin.

flashcards.definition: Acid + alkali → salt + water is exothermic; the mixture warms up.
flashcards.example: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O gives out heat.

flashcards.definition: On a pathway diagram, Eₐ runs from reactants up to the peak; ΔH runs from reactants to products (Extended).
flashcards.example: The ΔH arrow for an exothermic reaction points downwards and is labelled negative.

questions.stem: What happens during an exothermic reaction?
choices: Energy is absorbed from the surroundings, so the temperature falls
There is no overall energy change
Energy is transferred to the surroundings, so the temperature rises
Energy is absorbed from the surroundings, so the temperature rises
questions.explanation: Exothermic means energy leaves the reaction and enters the surroundings — a thermometer in the mixture shows a rise. A temperature fall signals an endothermic reaction.

choices: Neutralising an acid with an alkali
questions.explanation: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ needs continuous heating — energy is taken in, so it is endothermic. Combustion, neutralisation and respiration all release energy and are exothermic.

questions.stem: On a reaction pathway diagram for an exothermic reaction, how are the products shown?
choices: At a lower energy than the reactants
At a higher energy than the reactants
At the same energy as the reactants
At the top of the hump
questions.explanation: In an exothermic reaction energy is released, so the products end up with LESS energy than the reactants — the products' line sits lower. The top of the hump is the activated complex, not the products.

questions.stem: For an exothermic reaction, the value of ΔH is: (Extended tier)
questions.explanation: ΔH = energy of products − energy of reactants. Products are lower in energy in an exothermic reaction, so ΔH is negative. Positive ΔH means endothermic.

questions.stem: What is the activation energy of a reaction? (Extended tier)
choices: The total energy released when the products form
The energy difference between reactants and products
The minimum energy colliding particles must have for a reaction to occur
The energy stored in the products' bonds
questions.explanation: Eₐ is the minimum energy needed for a collision to succeed — the height of the hump from the reactants' level. The reactant-product difference is ΔH, not Eₐ.

questions.stem: Which statement about bond breaking and bond making is correct? (Extended tier)
choices: Both breaking and making bonds release energy
Breaking bonds releases energy; making bonds absorbs it
Both breaking and making bonds absorb energy
Breaking bonds absorbs energy; making bonds releases it
questions.explanation: Pulling atoms apart takes energy in (breaking is endothermic); joining atoms lets energy out (making is exothermic). The balance of the two gives the overall ΔH.

questions.stem: On a reaction pathway diagram, the activation energy is shown by an arrow: (Extended tier)
choices: From the reactants' level up to the top of the hump
From the reactants' level to the products' level
From the products' level up to the top of the hump
questions.explanation: Eₐ measures how far the reactants must climb to reach the activated complex — reactants to peak. The reactants-to-products arrow is ΔH, the common mix-up.

questions.stem: What is the unit of ΔH used at IGCSE? (Extended tier)
questions.explanation: Enthalpy changes are quoted per mole of reaction, in kJ/mol. J/s is a unit of power and °C measures temperature, not energy change.

questions.stem: Using the bond energies H–H $436$, Cl–Cl $242$ and H–Cl $431\text{ kJ/mol}$, what is ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl? (Extended tier)
questions.explanation: Bonds broken: $436 + 242 = 678\text{ kJ/mol}$. Bonds made: $2 \times 431 = 862\text{ kJ/mol}$ (two H–Cl bonds). ΔH $= 678 - 862 = -184\text{ kJ/mol}$ — negative, so the reaction is exothermic. Forgetting the factor of 2 gives $-92$.

questions.stem: Using C–H $412$, O=O $496$, C=O $743$ and O–H $463\text{ kJ/mol}$, what is ΔH for CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O? (Extended tier)
questions.explanation: Broken: 4 C–H + 2 O=O $= 4 \times 412 + 2 \times 496 = 2640\text{ kJ/mol}$. Made: 2 C=O + 4 O–H $= 2 \times 743 + 4 \times 463 = 3338\text{ kJ/mol}$. ΔH $= 2640 - 3338 = -698\text{ kJ/mol}$. $+698$ is the sign-flipped answer; $-1194$ forgets that 2O₂ means two O=O bonds.

questions.stem: Using N≡N $944$, H–H $436$ and N–H $388\text{ kJ/mol}$, what is ΔH for N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃? (Extended tier)
questions.explanation: Broken: 1 N≡N + 3 H–H $= 944 + 3 \times 436 = 2252\text{ kJ/mol}$. Made: 6 N–H (2NH₃ has six bonds) $= 6 \times 388 = 2328\text{ kJ/mol}$. ΔH $= 2252 - 2328 = -76\text{ kJ/mol}$, slightly exothermic — the bond counting (three H₂, six N–H) is where the errors creep in.

questions.stem: A sports cold pack mixes ammonium nitrate with water and immediately feels cold. Why?
choices: The dissolving is exothermic, releasing cold energy
The dissolving is endothermic — it takes in energy from the surroundings, including your skin
The water evaporates inside the sealed pack
The ammonium nitrate freezes the water
questions.explanation: Dissolving ammonium nitrate is endothermic: it absorbs energy from its surroundings, so anything touching the pack loses heat and feels cold. 'Cold energy' is not a thing — cold is the REMOVAL of energy.

questions.stem: In a reaction, breaking the reactant bonds absorbs $1256\text{ kJ/mol}$ and forming the product bonds releases $1486\text{ kJ/mol}$. What is ΔH? (Extended tier)
questions.explanation: ΔH = broken − made $= 1256 - 1486 = -230\text{ kJ/mol}$. More energy is released than absorbed, so the reaction is exothermic and the sign is negative. $+2742$ adds the two values instead of subtracting.

choices: Neutralisation of hydrochloric acid by sodium hydroxide
questions.explanation: Neutralisation releases energy and the mixture warms — exothermic. Thermal decomposition, dissolving NH₄NO₃ and photosynthesis all take energy in and are endothermic.

questions.stem: A reaction absorbs $2840\text{ kJ/mol}$ to break its reactant bonds and releases $2450\text{ kJ/mol}$ when its product bonds form. What are ΔH and the reaction type? (Extended tier)
questions.explanation: ΔH $= 2840 - 2450 = +390\text{ kJ/mol}$. More energy was absorbed breaking bonds than released making them, so the reaction takes in energy overall — positive ΔH and endothermic. The sign and the type must agree.
